</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS5.6" class="ltx_text">III-E</span> </span><span id="S3.SS5.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Candidate Validation and Trusted Selection</span></h3>

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The mapping interface prevents the agent from directly expressing illegal
native code, but surface validation alone is not sufficient evidence that a
candidate is correct. The framework therefore admits a plan to incumbent
selection only after compiler legality checks, execution, numerical
verification, and target-specific evidence collection.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compiler legality.</span>
ACT first resolves all mapping decisions and checks their joint constraints.
These checks cover tensor shapes, on-chip capacity, complete computation and
output coverage, reductions, and cross-operation dependencies. The generated
backend then owns instruction selection, memory management, synchronization,
and target code generation. An invalid mapping is rejected before execution;
the agent never repairs native code.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Numerical verification.</span>
Every candidate executes on the input bundle fixed by its workload contract,
and the evaluator compares the complete output with an independent oracle.
Data preparation required by a mapping remains inside the measured execution
boundary. For PLENA mappings that vary precision, the workload contract fixes
the acceptable numerical policy, so the agent cannot trade away correctness
to improve performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Gemmini evidence and objective.</span>
Gemmini candidates additionally undergo a separate kernel-delimited dynamic
trace. The trace establishes that the candidate consumes the workload inputs
and produces the complete output through Gemmini execution rather than a host
fallback.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Each evaluated mapping is compiled into a bare-metal executable and run on the
Gemmini FPGA. The measurement harness uses <span id="S3.SS5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">rdcycle</span> to delimit the
complete kernel execution, including any view, repacking, or bias preparation
required by the workload ABI and the Rocket-side command-issue overhead. The
measured executable is the same program subjected to full-output verification
and dynamic tracing, so correctness, provenance, and performance refer to the
same mapping.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Gemmini’s performance objective is the cycle count measured directly on the
FPGA. This provides a direct hardware cycle measurement rather than an
analytic or simulator-derived cost estimate. Feedback also reports factual
structural properties of the evaluated schedule, including external-transfer
bytes, Gemmini command counts, useful and padded MACs, operand reuse, and
scratchpad and accumulator occupancy. These properties help the agent
interpret why one mapping is faster than another.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS5.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PLENA evidence and objective.</span>
A PLENA resolved plan is lowered to target code and executed by PLENA’s
event-driven transaction-level emulator <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>. The emulator
models compute execution, instruction scheduling, and memory transactions at
cycle granularity, including detailed HBM timing, and reports a
cycle-approximate execution latency. We minimize this latency, which reflects
the dependency stalls and overlap of the realized multi-engine schedule.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS5.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Trusted selection.</span>
<span id="S3.SS5.p8.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span> and searched candidates follow the same target-specific path.
After each evaluation, the controller replaces the incumbent only when the
new candidate is verified and strictly improves the primary metric. Otherwise,
the previous incumbent remains. Gemmini compares board-measured cycles, while
PLENA compares transaction-level latency. The agent can propose mappings and
interpret feedback, but it cannot change the correctness policy, performance
metric, or final selection rule. Thus, neural reasoning influences which
mappings are explored without controlling how their native code, correctness,
or performance is judged.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">IV </span><span id="S4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Evaluation</span></h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">IV-A</span> </span><span id="S4.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Setup</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Accelerator platforms.</span>
We evaluate <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> on Gemmini and PLENA. For Gemmini, we use the
<span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GemminiRocketConfig</span> provided by Chipyard
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>, whose default Gemmini configuration sets
<span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">DIM=16</span> and instantiates a <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\times 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times 16</annotation></semantics></math> systolic array. We build the
bitstream of this SoC with Vivado 2022.2, generate its software image with
PetaLinux 2022.2, and deploy the resulting system on a Xilinx ZC706 FPGA
evaluation board. We obtain Gemmini performance measurements from this
physical implementation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For PLENA, we use the authors’ official RTL release and the transaction-level
mode of their official simulator <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>. The
simulator executes compiled assembly against an explicit memory layout and
produces both numerical outputs and simulated latency. Following KernelCraft’s
PLENA evaluation methodology <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, we use the
simulator-reported cycle count as the performance metric.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model and workloads.</span>
All agentic experiments use DeepSeek-V4-Flash <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>.
Across both accelerators, we adopt the applicable benchmark definitions and
input shapes published by KernelCraft <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>. We refer to
each workload–input-shape combination as a <em id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">workload instance</em>.
For each workload instance, Neural and <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> receive the same
maximum number of agent iterations, giving both methods an equal search
budget.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span> </span><span id="S4.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Gemmini Results</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison.</span>
We compare three methods across 20 instances from BatchMatMul, GEMM,
GEMV, and Linear. <em id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Neural</em> follows KernelCraft’s direct agentic workflow
and generates a native kernel for each instance. <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span> is the
compiler’s default legal mapping and requires no model inference.
<span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> reports the best verified mapping found by its
feedback-directed search. Every method uses the same workload inputs,
correctness oracle, and execution boundary. For a successful Neural run, we
report the correct kernel with the lowest cycle count. We report the token
usage of the complete inference trajectory for both successful and failed
runs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mapping search improves performance beyond the verified
default.</span>
<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span> produces a correct executable mapping for every
instance, so its gap to <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> isolates the optimization
headroom available after legality and code generation have been handled.
Figure <a href="#S3.F5.sf1" title="In Fig. 5 ‣ III-D2 PLENA: Conditional Symbolic Region Search ‣ III-D Adapting Search Granularity to the Target ‣ III Design ‣ Rethinking Agentic Kernel Generation for Emerging Accelerators" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5a</span></a> shows that this headroom depends strongly on
the workload family. <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>’s geometric-mean speedup over
<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span> is <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="8.54\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>8.54</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8.54\times</annotation></semantics></math> for GEMM, <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3.44\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.44</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.44\times</annotation></semantics></math> for BatchMatMul,
<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3.06\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.06</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.06\times</annotation></semantics></math> for Linear, and <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.40\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.40</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.40\times</annotation></semantics></math> for GEMV. The matrix–matrix
workloads expose the largest benefit from workload-specific tiling and reuse
decisions. Across the complete suite, <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> improves every
instance and achieves a <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3.34\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.34</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.34\times</annotation></semantics></math> geometric-mean speedup over
<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The same figure reveals a second effect: direct native-kernel generation has
uneven reliability across workload families. Neural succeeds on all five
BatchMatMul instances, four of five GEMMs, two of five GEMVs, and three
of five Linear instances. <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> retains a correct verified
incumbent on all 20 instances. It also achieves a lower cycle count than
Neural’s best correct kernel in each of Neural’s 14 successful runs, with a
<math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.79\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.79</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.79\times</annotation></semantics></math> geometric-mean speedup. The compiler boundary therefore supplies
complete workload coverage while preserving enough mapping freedom to
outperform both the default mapping and direct agentic generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Focused mapping search reduces inference cost.</span>
Figure <a href="#S3.F5.sf2" title="In Fig. 5 ‣ III-D2 PLENA: Conditional Symbolic Region Search ‣ III-D Adapting Search Granularity to the Target ‣ III Design ‣ Rethinking Agentic Kernel Generation for Emerging Accelerators" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5b</span></a> shows that <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> consumes 132K tokens
per instance on average, compared with 459K for Neural, a 71.2%
reduction. Neural’s six failed trajectories average 533K tokens, 24.6% more
than its successful trajectories at 428K. These failures are expensive
searches: the direct workflow continues spending inference on a native
realization and finishes without a usable kernel.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The largest savings occur on Linear (81.4%) and GEMV (76.4%), the two
lowest-success families for Neural. The pattern links reliability and cost:
direct generation spends its largest budgets in the families it handles least
reliably. The shorter <span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> trajectories also produce the fastest
kernel on every instance. Reusing the compiler’s machine realization
focuses inference and performance feedback on mapping choices, giving each
trajectory a smaller search responsibility and a verified result.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">IV-C</span> </span><span id="S4.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">PLENA Results</span></h3>

<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2608.00894v1/plena_results.png" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/200;" width="476" height="200" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 6: </span>PLENA results across 36 workload instances. Panel (a) reports
kernel cycles normalized to <span id="S4.F6.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span>; lower is better. Panel (b)
reports complete-trajectory inference tokens. A red cross marks a Neural run
that produced no correct kernel. For <span id="S4.F6.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>, both panels report the
lowest-cycle result among three search runs, with tokens taken from the same
run. <span id="S4.F6.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span> requires no model inference.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison.</span>
We compare the same three methods across 36 instances from 12 workload
families spanning matrix, normalization, activation, and attention
computations. Neural again generates a native kernel for each instance,
whereas <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span> and <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> use the reusable PLENA backend.
For Neural, we report the correct kernel with the lowest cycle count and the
token usage of the complete trajectory whether or not it succeeds. For
<span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>, we report the lowest-cycle verified result among three search
runs and the token usage of the trajectory that produced that result.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Symbolic coverage exposes optimization headroom.</span>
Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Fig. 6 ‣ IV-C PLENA Results ‣ IV Evaluation ‣ Rethinking Agentic Kernel Generation for Emerging Accelerators" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>(a) shows that <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> improves
<span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span> on 34 of 36 instances and matches it on the remaining
two, achieving a <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.10\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.10</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.10\times</annotation></semantics></math> geometric-mean speedup across the suite. The
largest family-level gains occur on GEMM (<math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.24\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.24</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.24\times</annotation></semantics></math>), GEMV (<math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.20\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.20</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.20\times</annotation></semantics></math>),
and FlashAttention (<math id="S4.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.18\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.18</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.18\times</annotation></semantics></math>), where tiling, data placement, and reuse
create substantial mapping headroom beyond the conservative default.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The same figure reveals a second effect: direct native-kernel generation has
much lower coverage. Neural produces a correct kernel on all three LayerNorm,
RMSNorm, SiLU, and Softmax instances, but on none of the 24 instances
from the other eight families. This coverage gap coincides with mapping-surface
complexity. All 12 Neural successes occur on instances exposing at most
ten free mapping knobs, whereas Neural fails on all 21 instances exposing
more than ten. <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> improves <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span> on every one of these
21 higher-dimensional instances, achieving a <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.11\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.11</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.11\times</annotation></semantics></math> geometric-mean
speedup, while retaining a correct verified incumbent on all 36 instances.
On the 12 instances where Neural succeeds, the two methods are
performance-competitive: <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> is faster on seven and Neural on five,
while Neural is <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.02\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.02</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.02\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster in geometric mean.
This comparison is necessarily conditioned on Neural success. On the other 24
instances, <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> still achieves a <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.12\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.12</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.12\times</annotation></semantics></math> geometric-mean
speedup over <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span>, converting the portion of the suite with no
Neural result into both complete coverage and measurable optimization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Focused search avoids costly failed trajectories.</span>
Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Fig. 6 ‣ IV-C PLENA Results ‣ IV Evaluation ‣ Rethinking Agentic Kernel Generation for Emerging Accelerators" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>(b) shows that <span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> consumes 1.71M
tokens per instance on average, compared with 3.72M for Neural, a 54.2%
reduction. Its average inference cost is likewise lower, at $0.070 per
instance versus $0.201 for Neural, a 65.1% reduction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The savings are concentrated in the instances that direct generation
cannot complete. Across Neural’s 24 failed trajectories, <span id="S4.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> uses
1.43M tokens per instance versus 4.58M for Neural, a 68.9% reduction,
while still returning a verified kernel. On the 12 successful Neural
instances, Neural instead uses fewer tokens, 2.01M versus 2.27M. Thus,
PLENA’s suite-level savings do not come from shortening every search. They come
from reusing the backend’s machine realization on the instances where a
direct agent otherwise spends a long trajectory without producing a usable
result.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS4.6" class="ltx_text">IV-D</span> </span><span id="S4.SS4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Cross-Platform Summary</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Across both targets, <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>’s benefits are consistent along three
dimensions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Performance over the symbolic baseline.</span>
<span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> achieves a <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3.34\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.34</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.34\times</annotation></semantics></math> geometric-mean improvement over
<span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span> on Gemmini and a <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.10\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.10</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.10\times</annotation></semantics></math> improvement on PLENA. It
improves 54 of the 56 instances and matches the baseline on the
remaining two.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Token efficiency.</span>
Relative to Neural, <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> reduces full-suite token usage by 71.2%
on Gemmini and 54.2% on PLENA.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Complete correctness coverage.</span>
<span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> returns a correct verified kernel on 20/20 Gemmini and 36/36
PLENA instances, achieving 100% coverage on both platforms. Neural
succeeds on only 14/20 (70.0%) and 12/36 (33.3%), respectively—26/56
(46.4%) instances overall.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Together, these results show that placing neural search inside a verified
compiler boundary consistently improves the symbolic starting point while
reducing search cost and preserving complete workload coverage.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">V </span><span id="S5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Discussion</span></h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">V-A</span> </span><span id="S5.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sensitivity to Model Capability</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An alternative explanation for our results is that Neural is disadvantaged by
an insufficiently capable model. Existing accelerator-kernel benchmarks do not
establish a monotonic capability ordering, as task completion and optimization
quality are not perfectly correlated <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>. We therefore
perform a controlled within-family ablation, replacing Flash with Pro, which
DeepSeek-V4 positions as the stronger configuration for challenging
tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We construct a capability-stratified set of six Gemmini instances from the
Flash results. The set includes an easy control (BatchMatMul C2), two
intermediate instances (GEMM C1 and C4), a difficult but solvable boundary
case (GEMV C5), an instance near Flash’s success boundary (Linear C4), and
a ceiling probe on which Flash fails (GEMV C3). For a uniform
one-result-per-instance comparison, we report the first run (seed 1) for
each model–method pair. Flash and Pro candidates are replayed using the same
board timing harness. Figure <a href="#S5.F7" title="Fig. 7 ‣ V-A Sensitivity to Model Capability ‣ V Discussion ‣ Rethinking Agentic Kernel Generation for Emerging Accelerators" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> summarizes the results;
each bar reports that run, and crosses directly denote failed Neural
trajectories.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2608.00894v1/gemmini_model_ablation.svg" id="S5.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/398;" width="476" height="398"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 7: </span>Gemmini model-capability ablation. (a) <span id="S5.F7.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>: Flash vs.
Pro. (b) Neural: Flash vs. Pro. (c, d) Pro Neural vs. <span id="S5.F7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>-Flash in
cycles and API cost, respectively. Crosses indicate failed runs. BM, MM, MV,
and LN abbreviate BatchMatMul, GEMM, GEMV, and Linear.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The compiler-mediated result is insensitive to the model
upgrade.</span>
For <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>, five of the six instances differ by at most 0.1%
between Flash and Pro. Pro improves GEMM C4 by 4.7%, but its geometric-mean
cycle count across all six instances is only 0.8% lower, and both models
retain a verified result throughout. In contrast, substituting Pro raises the
geometric-mean API cost by <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="17.0\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>17.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">17.0\times</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, on Gemmini’s enumerable mapping
spaces, Flash already crosses the capability threshold needed to guide the
search. Beyond this point, the symbolic mapping engine, compiler-owned
realization, and verified incumbent selection determine the returned kernel
more strongly than additional model capacity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Additional capability affects direct generation, but not
monotonically.</span>
Pro recovers a correct direct kernel for GEMV C3, where Flash fails, showing that
additional capability can move the success boundary. It does not uniformly
improve the task, however: Pro fails on Linear C4, which Flash solves. Among the
four instances that both Neural variants solve, Pro is faster on
BatchMatMul C2 and GEMV C5 but slower on both GEMM instances; its geometric
mean cycle count is 10.2% higher than Flash’s. A stronger general model can
therefore solve a previously failed case without inducing a monotonic change in
kernel correctness or quality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A stronger direct Neural does not close the gap.</span>
The Pro Neural succeeds on five of six instances, whereas
<span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>-Flash returns a verified kernel for all six. Among the five
successful Neural runs, <span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>-Flash is faster on four and achieves a
<math id="S5.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.60\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.60</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.60\times</annotation></semantics></math> geometric-mean speedup. Pro Neural’s only win is 5.5%, while
<span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>’s largest advantage is <math id="S5.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3.01\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.01</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.01\times</annotation></semantics></math>. Moreover, Pro Neural costs
<math id="S5.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="5.92\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5.92</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.92\times</annotation></semantics></math> more than <span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>-Flash in geometric mean across all six
trajectories, including the money spent on the failed Linear C4 trajectory.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">These results separate the value of neural guidance from the value of a larger
model. Neural guidance remains useful for proposing performance-oriented mapping
directions, as shown by <span id="S5.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>’s improvement over <span id="S5.SS1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span>, but
once the model is sufficiently capable, upgrading it produces no measurable
kernel-quality benefit inside the symbolic boundary. We therefore use Flash for
the main evaluation: it preserves <span id="S5.SS1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>’s correctness and performance
at substantially lower inference cost. More broadly, these results suggest
that a symbolic boundary can make kernel quality less sensitive to model
capability once the model can navigate the exposed mapping space. This
conclusion is specific to the finite Gemmini mapping surfaces evaluated here.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">V-B</span> </span><span id="S5.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Neural Selection versus Random Sampling</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Gemmini exposes a finite legal mapping catalog, a natural alternative
is to sample mappings uniformly and retain the fastest measured candidate. We
ask whether Neural’s adaptive selection improves over this baseline under the
same evaluation budget.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate both policies on all 20 Gemmini instances. Random samples
legal candidates uniformly without replacement. Neural uses the measured cycles
and structural observations from previous trials to choose each subsequent
candidate. Both policies use the same exhaustively enumerated and verified
catalog, share the same compiler-default baseline, and receive at most 12 unique
candidate evaluations. Values and ranks of untried candidates remain hidden,
and the catalog is independently permuted on every Neural turn. The harness
returns the fastest candidate that each policy actually evaluates. The sole
experimental variable is therefore whether previous measurements direct the
remaining evaluation budget.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Neural selection reduces tail regret.</span>
With measured board cycles as feedback, Neural reaches the known exhaustive
optimum on all 20 instances, compared with 14 for Random. Under the 0.25%
measurement dead band, Neural wins six head-to-head comparisons and ties the
remaining 14; Random’s worst-case regret is 4.89%. All six Neural wins occur in
catalogs containing 31–55 candidates, where the 12-evaluation budget covers
only 21.8–38.7% of the legal surface. These results show that adaptive
selection converts the same compile-and-measure budget into more effective
coverage and removes the observed tail of missed mappings. We therefore use
Neural to direct mapping selection. These results are scoped to the small
enumerable catalogs evaluated here; larger search spaces require separate
evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">V-C</span> </span><span id="S5.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Implications for Agentic Design-Space Exploration</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The broader implication of <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> is a new programming interface for
hardware-aware kernel programming and optimization. Direct agentic generation
asks a policy to produce a complete native program, coupling workload
mapping with instruction selection, memory management, synchronization, and
other fixed machine rules.
In <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>, the mapping surface, symbolic completion, and verified
evaluator instead expose a typed interface from workload-level decisions to
measured executable candidates. This interface is not intrinsically neural:
an LLM agent, a heuristic, or a conventional search algorithm can all propose
mapping intents while using the same compiler-owned realization and trusted
selection path. Accelerator kernel generation can therefore be reformulated
from end-to-end synthesis of a native program into design-space exploration
bounded by a compiler-defined symbolic interface.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This reformulation separates the intelligence used to explore a space from the
infrastructure that defines and validates it. A search policy need not learn
how to encode a legal DMA sequence or maintain configuration state before it
can test a tiling, placement, precision, or overlap hypothesis. It instead
receives workload-conditioned decision domains, proposes a point or region,
and obtains correctness, performance, and structural feedback for the legal
plans completed by the compiler. Different proposal policies can consequently
be compared or combined without changing the workload contract, native code
generator, evaluator, or correctness boundary. The symbolic interface is thus
both a correctness boundary and a reusable DSE substrate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">It also opens a direct path toward a stronger evolutionary harness for agentic
DSE. AlphaEvolve demonstrates how an archive of evaluated programs, automated
fitness, and LLM-generated variations can sustain long-horizon algorithmic
search <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>; ShinkaEvolve further improves this pattern
with exploration-aware parent selection, novelty filtering, adaptive model
selection, and accumulated search knowledge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>. A
<span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> harness could apply these mechanisms at two levels: evolve
verified mapping intents directly, or evolve heuristics that generate intents,
rather than evolving unrestricted native programs. It could maintain an archive
of evaluated mappings, select parents by performance and diversity, mutate or
recombine typed decisions, and let symbolic completion legalize each offspring
before execution. Such a design would preserve <span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>’s compiler
boundary while allowing evolutionary, heuristic, and neural operators to share
experience and explore larger conditional mapping spaces more efficiently.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VI </span><span id="S6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Related Work</span></h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mapping-space search and autotuning.</span>
Tensor compilers such as TVM, Ansor, and MetaSchedule and accelerator mapping
tools such as Timeloop and MAESTRO share the same basic abstraction: a
manually designed scheduling or mapping space is explored by a search policy
and scored by execution, an analytical model, or a learned surrogate
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>. <span id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> retains this
separation between space and policy, but derives the executable backend and its
workload-conditioned legal surface from machine specifications, then verifies
realized kernels on the target path.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Agentic accelerator kernel generation.</span>
A separate line of work asks LLM agents to write and optimize accelerator
kernels themselves. KernelCraft generates close-to-metal programs for emerging
accelerators, and AutoComp uses execution feedback to optimize code for tensor
accelerators <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>. AccelOpt directly
rewrites Trainium NKI kernels using measured profiles, beam search, and an
optimization memory distilled from slow–fast kernel pairs
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>. Together, these systems show that agents can produce
correct, high-performance kernels for specialized
accelerators, not only GPUs. They keep kernel construction and machine
realization inside the agentic loop. <span id="S6.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> instead asks the agent for
uses a generated backend to complete legal choices and emit native code,
making the machine realization reusable across workloads.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VII </span><span id="S7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Conclusion</span></h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span>, a compiler-mediated framework that separates
reusable machine realization from per-workload mapping search for emerging
accelerators. A generated backend exposes a workload-conditioned mapping
surface, completes and legalizes proposed mappings, and lowers them to native
code. A neural agent uses verified correctness and performance feedback to
direct exploration. Across 20 Gemmini and 36 PLENA workload instances,
<span id="S7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> returns a correct verified kernel for all 56 instances;
direct Neural succeeds on 26. <span id="S7.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Zomboss</span> improves <span id="S7.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span> on 54
instances and matches it on two, with geometric-mean speedups of
<math id="S7.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3.34\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.34</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.34\times</annotation></semantics></math> on Gemmini and <math id="S7.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.10\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.10</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.10\times</annotation></semantics></math> on PLENA. It also reduces inference
tokens relative to Neural by 71.2% and 54.2%, respectively. These results
establish a compiler-defined symbolic interface as an effective boundary for
agentic kernel generation. The boundary turns native kernel synthesis into
verified design-space exploration and exposes the same target realization to
neural, heuristic, evolutionary, and conventional search policies.</p>
</div>
</section>
